beef-steak-with-onions-puerto-rican-styl.title: Beef Steak with Onions, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Beef steak with onions, Puerto Rican style is a classic island dish featuring thinly sliced beef sautéed with onions, garlic, vinegar, soy sauce, and spices such as oregano and adobo. It is traditionally served with rice, beans, and fried plantains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the early 20th century when American military bases introduced U.S. cooking influences to Puerto Rico.
The traditional marinade uses vinegar and soy sauce, giving the meat a distinctive tangy‑salty flavor.
Onions are often caramelized, softening their bite and adding sweetness.
In Puerto Rico the steak is frequently accompanied by “mojo” sauce made from tomatoes, peppers, and spices.
It is a staple at family celebrations and street festivals.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Rich in heme iron and zinc, it supports immune function and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from onions
items.content: Onions supply quercetin and sulfur compounds with anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: The dish fits well into low‑carb diets as the main calories come from protein and fat.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Large portions of beef can raise cholesterol; choose lean cuts when possible.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Soy sauce and the marinade add salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Onion allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to onions or garlic.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Beef should reach an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F) to reduce food‑borne illness risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the steak thinly, serve hot with caramelized onions, rice, beans, and fried plantains. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime juice, and optional hot adobo sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked steak in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

content.title: About
content.content: Pimiento is a medium‑sized sweet pepper grown in warm regions. It comes in bright red, orange or yellow hues, has a crisp texture and a mildly sweet flavor. Pimiento is eaten fresh, roasted, grilled, and used in salads, sauces, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pimiento belongs to the nightshade family and is closely related to bell pepper.
It contains 3–4 times more vitamin C than an orange.
There are over 30 varieties of pimiento with different colors and shapes.
In traditional Mediterranean cuisine pimiento is often stuffed with rice and meat.
The seeds can be dried and ground into a spice – paprika.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and supports collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Pimiento is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peppers.

items.title: Capsaicin content
items.content: High amounts can irritate the stomach in sensitive people.

items.title: Pesticide residue
items.content: Choose organic or wash thoroughly to reduce exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pimiento can be eaten raw, sliced into salads, roasted in the oven, grilled, or stuffed. For tenderness it is often baked wrapped in foil. It pairs well with olive oil, garlic, and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pimiento in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer in a plastic bag or container. At room temperature it stays fresh for up to 5 days, and in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.
